title: Rheumatoid Arthritis & The Eye: A Comprehensive Ophthalmic Perspective
summary: Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) is a chronic systemic autoimmune disease primarily affecting joints, but its ocular manifestations are diverse and vision-threatening, ranging from common dry eye to severe necrotizing scleritis and peripheral ulcerative keratitis. Ophthalmologists play a critical role in diagnosis, monitoring, and management to prevent irreversible vision loss.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) is a chronic, systemic inflammatory autoimmune disease primarily characterized by symmetrical polyarthritis, leading to progressive joint destruction, deformity, and functional impairment. It predominantly affects small joints of the hands and feet. Beyond articular involvement, RA frequently manifests with extra-articular features, including significant ocular involvement, which can range from benign conditions like dry eye to severe, vision-threatening scleritis or peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK).

sections.title: 2.1 Epidemiological Details
content: **Prevalence:** ~0.5-1% of the adult population worldwide.
**Incidence:** Varies geographically, typically 20-50 cases per 100,000 adults per year.
**Demographics:** Predominantly affects women (female:male ratio 2-3:1).
**Age of Onset:** Most common between 40-60 years.
**Risk Factors:** Genetic predisposition (HLA-DRB1 alleles, especially shared epitope), smoking, obesity, periodontal disease, certain infections (e.g., Porphyromonas gingivalis), silica exposure.

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Symptoms (Ocular Focus)
content: **KCS:** Foreign body sensation, burning, stinging, gritty feeling, photophobia, blurred vision (fluctuating), increased reflex tearing followed by dryness.
**Episcleritis:** Acute onset mild redness, localized tenderness, mild discomfort (not severe pain), no significant vision change. Vessels blanch with phenylephrine.

**Scleritis (Anterior):** Severe, deep, boring pain radiating to brow/temple/jaw, tenderness to palpation, intense violaceous redness (non-blanching with phenylephrine), photophobia, lacrimation, decreased vision. Nodular type shows elevated, immobile nodule. Necrotizing type shows avascular patches, scleral thinning, potentially globe perforation.
**Scleritis (Posterior):** Often painless or vague orbital pain, proptosis, diplopia, reduced vision, serous retinal detachment, choroidal folds, disc edema, macular edema.
**PUK:** Severe pain, redness, photophobia, rapid decrease in vision, crescentic ulceration at the limbus, often with an epithelial defect and stromal melt. Can be sterile or secondarily infected.
**Anterior Uveitis:** Pain, photophobia, redness (circumlimbal flush), blurred vision, floaters.
**Hydroxychloroquine Retinopathy:** Asymptomatic early, paracentral scotomas, eventually central vision loss. Visual field defects (10-2), color vision changes.

sections.title: 6. Ocular Examination Findings
content: **KCS:** Decreased tear meniscus height, conjunctival injection, punctate epithelial erosions (fluorescein stain), positive Rose Bengal or Lissamine Green staining (conjunctival/corneal epithelial damage), reduced tear break-up time (TBUT <10s).
**Episcleritis:** Sectoral or diffuse redness, engorged episcleral vessels (move with conjunctival manipulation), easily blanch with 2.5% topical phenylephrine.

**Scleritis (Anterior):** Violaceous hue of sclera (non-blanching with phenylephrine), edema, vessel engorgement. Nodular: firm, tender, immobile scleral nodule. Necrotizing: areas of scleral thinning (blueish discoloration of underlying choroid), avascular patches, potentially exposed uvea, impending perforation.

**Scleritis (Posterior):** Normal anterior segment. Fundoscopy: disc edema, choroidal folds, serous retinal detachment, macular edema. B-scan ultrasonography is diagnostic: 'T-sign' (fluid in Tenon's capsule, thickening of choroid/sclera).
**PUK:** Ciliary injection, perilimbal crescentic corneal thinning/ulceration, epithelial defect, underlying stromal infiltrate. May see exposed Descemet's membrane, iris prolapse if perforated.
**Anterior Uveitis:** Keratic precipitates, anterior chamber cell and flare, posterior synechiae, iris nodules, band keratopathy, raised intraocular pressure.
**Hydroxychloroquine Retinopathy:** Early: subtle RPE mottling. Late: classic 'bull's eye' maculopathy (ring of RPE atrophy surrounding a relatively spared fovea).

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **1. Systemic Evaluation (Rheumatologist Referral):** Confirm RA diagnosis. Obtain detailed history of joint symptoms, systemic involvement.

**2. Serological Tests:**
    - Rheumatoid Factor (RF): Positive in 70-80% (non-specific).
    - Anti-cyclic Citrullinated Peptide (Anti-CCP) antibodies: Highly specific for RA (95-98%), prognostically significant.
    - Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) & C-Reactive Protein (CRP): Elevated during active inflammation.

**3. Ocular Surface Tests (for KCS):**
    - Schirmer's Test: <10mm wetting in 5 minutes (without anesthesia for basal secretion, with for reflex).
    - Tear Break-Up Time (TBUT): <10 seconds.
    - Ocular Surface Staining: Fluorescein (corneal epithelial defects), Lissamine Green/Rose Bengal (conjunctival & corneal devitalized cells).

**4. Imaging for Scleritis/PUK:**
    - B-scan Ultrasonography: Essential for posterior scleritis ('T-sign', choroidal thickening, fluid in Tenon's).
    - UBM (Ultrasound Biomicroscopy): High-resolution imaging of anterior segment, useful for anterior scleritis extent.
    - OCT: Retinal/choroidal changes in posterior scleritis, early HCQ retinopathy (parafoveal RPE/photoreceptor atrophy).
**5. Visual Field Testing:** 10-2 visual field for hydroxychloroquine retinopathy screening (early paracentral scotomas).
**6. Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF):** Used in HCQ screening, shows RPE atrophy.
**7. Angiography (FFA/ICG):** In rare cases of retinal vasculitis.

sections.title: 9. Staging/Grading (Ocular Specificity)
content: **RA Disease Activity:** Assessed by rheumatologist using tools like DAS28 (Disease Activity Score 28), CDAI (Clinical Disease Activity Index) which guide systemic therapy.
**KCS Severity:** Graded by symptoms (OSDI), Schirmer's, staining patterns.

**Scleritis Grading:** 
    - **Anatomical:** Anterior (diffuse, nodular, necrotizing), Posterior.
    - **Inflammatory:** Active, quiescent.
    - **Severity:** Mild (diffuse/nodular anterior), Severe (necrotizing, posterior, PUK).

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment (Ocular RA)
content:
**1. Keratoconjunctivitis Sicca (KCS):**
    - **Initial:** Preservative-free artificial tears (e.g., Refresh Optive, Systane Ultra) q2-4h.
    - **Moderate:** Topical cyclosporine 0.05% (Restasis) BID or 0.09% (Cequa) BID; topical lifitegrast 5% (Xiidra) BID.
    - **Severe:** Punctal plugs (silicone or collagen), topical corticosteroids (e.g., loteprednol 0.2% BID for short courses), amniotic membranes, autologous serum tears, oral omega-3 fatty acids.

**2. Episcleritis:**
    - **Mild:** Usually self-limiting. Cool compresses, topical NSAIDs (e.g., Ketorolac 0.4% QID).
    - **Persistent:** Mild topical corticosteroids (e.g., Loteprednol 0.2% BID-QID) for short duration, oral NSAIDs (e.g., Ibuprofen 400-600mg TID).

**3. Scleritis (Anterior Diffuse/Nodular):**
    - **Systemic NSAIDs:** First-line. Indomethacin 25-50mg TID-QID, Naproxen 250-500mg BID, Flurbiprofen 100mg TID. Full trial for 2-3 weeks.
    - **Systemic Corticosteroids:** If NSAIDs fail or severe. Prednisone 1mg/kg/day (max 60-80mg/day), then slowly taper.

**4. Scleritis (Necrotizing / Posterior) & PUK:**
    - **Urgent Immunosuppression:** This is an ocular emergency.
        - **High-dose Systemic Corticosteroids:** Prednisone 1mg/kg/day (up to 80mg/day) for several weeks, then taper.
        - **Immunomodulatory Therapy (DMARDs):** Often initiated concurrently. Methotrexate (7.5-25mg/week), Azathioprine (1-3mg/kg/day), Mycophenolate Mofetil (1-2g/day), Cyclosporine (2.5-5mg/kg/day).
        - **Biologics:** If refractory to conventional DMARDs. TNF-α inhibitors (e.g., Infliximab, Adalimumab, Etanercept), Rituximab (anti-CD20), Tocilizumab (anti-IL-6R), Abatacept (CTLA-4-Ig). Selection based on systemic RA control and specific ocular manifestation.
    - **Topical Corticosteroids:** *Cautious use for PUK.* May worsen corneal melt unless combined with strong systemic immunosuppression. Prednisolone acetate 1% (QID-hourly) can be used, but risks must be weighed.

**5. Hydroxychloroquine Retinopathy:**
    - **Discontinuation of HCQ:** If retinopathy is confirmed, stop medication immediately to prevent progression.
    - **Regular Screening:** Annual screening after 5 years of use (or earlier if high risk - >5mg/kg/day, renal disease, concomitant tamoxifen use). Includes SD-OCT (parafoveal outer retinal thinning), 10-2 visual fields, FAF.

sections.title: 11. Surgical Techniques (Ocular RA)
content:
**1. Corneal Perforation (PUK):**
    - **Cyanoacrylate Glue Application:** For small perforations (<3mm) to seal the defect and allow healing.
    - **Lamellar or Penetrating Keratoplasty:** For larger perforations or extensive corneal melt. May require tectonic patch graft (donor sclera, cornea, fascia lata) to restore structural integrity.
    - **Amniotic Membrane Transplant:** Can aid in surface healing and reduce inflammation.
**2. Punctal Occlusion:** Punctal plugs (silicone or dissolvable collagen) for severe KCS.
**3. Cataract Surgery:** For steroid-induced cataracts, typically phacoemulsification with IOL implantation.
**4. Glaucoma Surgery:** For steroid-induced or uveitic glaucoma (trabeculectomy, glaucoma drainage device) if medically uncontrolled.

sections.title: 12. Complications & Prognosis
content: **Scleritis:** Scleral thinning, staphyloma formation, anterior uveitis, glaucoma, cataract, globe perforation (especially necrotizing type). Vision loss is a significant risk.
**PUK:** Corneal perforation, secondary infection, irregular astigmatism, permanent vision loss, globe loss (rare).
**KCS:** Chronic discomfort, recurrent corneal erosions, infectious keratitis, corneal scarring, vision impairment.
**Hydroxychloroquine Retinopathy:** Irreversible central vision loss if not detected and medication stopped early.
**General:** Poorly controlled systemic RA increases risk of severe ocular complications. Early diagnosis and aggressive systemic immunosuppression improve ocular prognosis.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: **Severe, Deep Boring Ocular Pain:** Highly suggestive of scleritis, especially if unresponsive to topical analgesics.
**Violaceous Redness of the Sclera (Non-blanching):** Pathognomonic for scleritis.
**Scleral Thinning / Avascular Patches:** Indicates necrotizing scleritis, high risk of perforation.
**Crescentic Perilimbal Corneal Ulceration (PUK):** Imminent risk of corneal perforation and globe loss.
**Sudden Decrease in Vision, Diplopia, Proptosis (without anterior segment inflammation):** Suggests posterior scleritis, requiring urgent investigation.
**New or Worsening Visual Field Defects (especially paracentral):** May indicate hydroxychloroquine retinopathy progression, necessitating drug cessation.

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls
content: Scleritis pain is often worse at night and wakes patients from sleep.
Differentiating episcleritis (blanches with phenylephrine) from scleritis (does not blanch) is crucial.
Necrotizing scleritis and PUK are true ocular emergencies requiring prompt and aggressive systemic immunosuppression, often with a rheumatologist.
Always inquire about systemic symptoms (joint pain, stiffness, fatigue) in patients presenting with unexplained recurrent or severe ocular inflammation.
Hydroxychloroquine retinopathy is irreversible; emphasize meticulous screening and patient education.
B-scan ultrasonography is indispensable for diagnosing posterior scleritis and orbital inflammation.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: Recent advances in RA management, particularly the development of biologics (e.g., TNF-α inhibitors like Infliximab, Adalimumab; IL-6 receptor blockers like Tocilizumab; B-cell inhibitors like Rituximab), have significantly improved systemic disease control and, consequently, reduced the incidence and severity of severe ocular complications like scleritis and PUK. The **AAO guidelines for hydroxychloroquine retinopathy screening (2016, updated 2021)** have standardized surveillance, emphasizing SD-OCT and 10-2 visual fields as primary screening tools, leading to earlier detection and prevention of severe vision loss. Ongoing research focuses on personalized medicine approaches, including identifying biomarkers for predicting ocular involvement and response to specific therapies.

sections.title: 17. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
content: **Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA):** The most common systemic rheumatic disease in children, with significant ocular involvement.

**Chronic Anterior Uveitis:** Most frequent ocular manifestation in JIA, often asymptomatic, bilateral, and non-granulomatous. Can lead to irreversible vision loss from band keratopathy, posterior synechiae, cataract, glaucoma, and macular edema.

**Screening for Uveitis in JIA:** All children with JIA require regular ophthalmic screening (slit-lamp examination) by an ophthalmologist, even in the absence of symptoms. Frequency depends on age of onset, specific JIA subtype (oligoarticular is highest risk), and presence of ANA antibodies.
**Treatment in JIA:** Topical corticosteroids are first-line for uveitis flares. Systemic immunosuppression (methotrexate, biologics) is often required for persistent or severe uveitis.
